land.text: the viscounty 'Founded by Xiong Yi: c. 1030 BC' at Danyang, a Zhou fief in the middle Han valley, in the original Chu area (modern Hubei) less the states it absorbed later

predecessors.note: A fief, not conquered land: Chu was enfeoffed as a viscounty under the Zhou and remained a nominal vassal until Xiong Tong 'proclaimed king: 706 or 703 BC'.

land.text: the whole state: 'In 223 BC, Wang Jian conquered the Chu capital Shouchun and captured King Fuchu of Chu'; 'By then, Chu had been completely conquered by Qin'

successors.note: The former Wu-Yue lands in the east were secured only in 222 BC: 'The following year, Wang Jian and Meng Wu led Qin forces to attack the Wuyue region' (Qin's wars page). Cliopatria ends Chu in 224; the pages give 223.

capitals.name: Danyang (Zhijiang, Hubei, or Xichuan, Henan)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Danyang (c. 1030 – c. 680 BC)'. The page gives two sites: 'located in today's Zhijiang, Hubei province' and 'at the junction of the Dan and Xi Rivers near present-day Xichuan County, Henan'; drawn at Zhijiang; coordinates approximate, no page opened for the site.

capitals.name: Ying (Jinancheng, Jingzhou)
capitals.note: 'the Chu capital moved south-east from Danyang to Ying' between 695 and 689 BC (infobox c. 680). Occupied by Wu in 506-505; in 504 the court 'temporarily moved the capital into the territory of the former state of Ruo'. Fell to Bai Qi in 278 BC. Coordinates: the Jinancheng site north of modern Jingzhou (gazetteer place Jingzhou 112.23 E 30.32 N), approximate.

capitals.name: Chen (Huaiyang)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Chen (陳) (278–241 BC)': the former state of Chen's capital Wanqiu, present-day Huaiyang (Zhoukou). Coordinates approximate (gazetteer place Zhoukou 114.63 E 33.63 N lies 25 km west).

capitals.name: Shouchun (Shou County)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Shouchun (壽春) (241–224 BC)'; 'Chu moved its capital east to Shouchun, farther away from the threat of Qin'; captured by Wang Jian in 223. Coordinates approximate (gazetteer place Huainan 116.98 E 32.63 N lies 20 km east). The infobox also lists Pengcheng without dates (the Chu–Han era, after this dossier).

rulers.name: Xiong Yong
rulers.note: The Chu page's ruler table; the viscounts before Xiong Yong (Xiong Yi, 11th century BC; Xiong Ai c. 977; Xiong Dan c. 941) have no reign spans and are left out.

rulers.name: King Wu (Xiong Tong / Xiong Da)
rulers.note: 'Xiong Tong proclaimed king: 706 or 703 BC' (infobox: Kingdom from 704 BC).

rulers.name: Zi'ao (Xiong Bi)
rulers.note: Reigned less than 20 days in 529 BC.

rulers.name: Fuchu
rulers.note: 'Captured by Qin troops and deposed' in 223 BC.

correction.text: the viscounty 'Founded by Xiong Yi: c. 1030 BC' with its capital Danyang, in 'its original area (modern Hubei)', without the Hubei states it absorbed later: E (863), Quan (704), Luo (690), Deng (678) and Yong (611)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the viscounty before Cliopatria's first shape (750 BC). The Chu page: 'Chu first consolidated its power by absorbing other states in its original area (modern Hubei), then it expanded into the north towards the North China Plain.' The shape is Cliopatria's 750 shape cut to Hubei and Hunan (about 172,000 km2 in the gazetteer's cells) less the circles of the five Hubei states the ledger annexes later, which the first version left inside the core (reviewer finding, 2026-10-18); about 138,000 km2 remain, still more than the early viscounty can have held. Soft edge: no page bounds it.

correction.text: the Han valley and the Jianghan plain around Danyang and Ying with E (863) already absorbed; Quan (704), Luo (690), Deng (678) and Yong (611) are still outside until the ledger annexes them

keyframe_review.note: 750-701. The first version was Cliopatria's 750 shape cut to Hubei and Hunan with the Hubei states inside it, so the ledger's gains of 704 to 611 changed nothing on the map (about 42,000 km2 of their circles lay inside the core; reviewer finding, 2026-10-18). The core now leaves Quan, Luo, Deng and Yong out and the gains add them in their years. Cliopatria's 750 shape (353,243 km2 from 109.3 to 118.9 E and 29.3 to 34.7 N) is Chu at the end of the Spring and Autumn period, not in 750: its northern and eastern part (southern Henan, Anhui, edges of Shaanxi, Chongqing and Jiangsu) is cut here and re-enters at the 480 keyframe (see the 480 ledger entry). That shape also covers Shangcai (Cai) and Huaiyang (Chen), which is why Cliopatria draws those two states displaced 80-120 km to the north (see their dossiers).

correction.text: the land Chu held in 700: the Hubei and Hunan core of Cliopatria's 700 shape with E (863) and Quan (704) absorbed, before the annexations of Luo (690), Deng (678) and Yong (611)

keyframe_review.note: 700-481. The first version kept the whole Cliopatria 700 shape (the end-of-period extent, identical to the 750 shape) less the Cai and Chen enclaves, so from 700 Chu already held the land of every state the ledger annexes from 688 to 512 and no event explained the step from 750 to 700 (reviewer finding, 2026-10-18). Now it is the Hubei and Hunan core only. From 690 the ledger adds Luo, Shen, Xi, Deng, Huang, Jiang, Liao, Lu (六), Jiang, Yong, Shuliao, Shuyong and Lai, then Chen (534-529), Cai (531) and Xu (512); in the gazetteer's cells those circles rebuild about 80,000 km2 of Cliopatria's southern Henan and Anhui extent by 512. The rest of that extent, about 165,000 km2 of Henan, Anhui and the Shaanxi, Chongqing and Jiangsu edges, is in Cliopatria's shape but no page dates its acquisition (the Chu page: 'then it expanded into the north towards the North China Plain'); it is left out until the 480 keyframe, where a confidence-1 ledger entry brings it in. Cai (Shangcai, Xincai) and Chen (Huaiyang) stay outside the Chu colour except in 531-529 and 534-529. Wu occupied Ying in 506-505 (hatched).

correction.text: the shape as drawn without Cai at Xiacai ('at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui') until 447 BC and without Chen at Huaiyang (Zhoukou) until 479 BC

keyframe_review.note: Same shape for 480-451. 'Chu annexed Chen in 479 BC', so Huaiyang is Chu from 479 (the first version cut only Cai and left Huaiyang in Chu's 480 shape while chen_-480 holds it for 480-479, a one-year double claim; reviewer finding, 2026-10-18). Cai had moved to Xiacai (Fengtai, by Huainan) and 'In 447 BC, King Hui of Chu conquered Cai completely' (Cai page), so Xiacai stays outside until 447. This keyframe is also where the land of Cliopatria's shape that no page dates (about 165,000 km2, see chu_-700 and the 480 ledger entry) enters. Xu (512) and the parts of the E, Yong and Hefei gain circles that lie outside Cliopatria's outline (about 17,000 km2 and Xu's own 5,600) are not carried into this shape.

376,813 km2 for 450-405, 23,500 km2 more than before: Chen (479) and Cai (447) absorbed, the bbox reaching Chen's old northern edge (34.87 N). Cliopatria adds them in 450, 29 and 3 years late; the ledger dates them.

389,794 km2 for 404-384, bbox east to 120.0 E and north to 35.8 N: Qi (Henan, 445), Ju (431, southern Shandong) and Pi ('After 418 BC', northern Jiangsu) from the page's list of states annexed by Chu.
389,769 km2 for 383-367: 25 km2 less than the previous shape, a neighbour's redraw (Zheng's row ends 367), no event.
389,794 km2 for 366-351: identical to the 404 shape; no event.
389,693 km2 for 350-338: 100 km2 less; no event on the pages. Zou ('About 348 BC') is in the ledger but is not visible in the shape; Cliopatria's Zhu (Zou) row ends 405.
389,617 km2 for 337-334: 76 km2 less; no event.

563,297 km2 for 333-316, bbox east to the coast (122.0 E): 'Yue was partitioned by Chu and Qi in 333 BC' (infobox 'Conquered by Chu: 333 BC'); the Chu page gives 334 or 333. Cliopatria's Yue row ends 334 and Minyue begins 333.

556,053 km2 for 315-285, 7,200 km2 less. The losses of these years on the King Huai page (Hanzhong in 312, a bridge that no page words; fx-52 K05: the King Huai page as served is a 480-word stub without these items, so none of the three quoted losses is confirmed there: Hanzhong in 312, 'Chongqiu of Pingyuan Commandery' in 301, 'eight Chu cities' in 299) are at the north-western edge; Cliopatria's western edge (109.3 E) never included Hanzhong, so the loss drawn here is a neighbour's redraw rather than Hanzhong. The ledger carries the three losses at confidence 1.

588,602 km2 for 284-278, the largest Chu shape (+32,500 km2): Chu's share of Song, 'partitioned by Qi, Chu and Wei' after 286 BC. Cliopatria adds it in 284, two years late. The pages do not say which part went to Chu; the ledger names the part of Song's last shape that Cliopatria gives Chu.

505,356 km2 for 277-248, western edge moved from 109.3 to 110.4 E (-83,000 km2): 'In 278 BC, he led the Qin army to capture Ying'. The lost land is Qin's from 278 (Cliopatria's Qin row). Lu, annexed 249, is not yet drawn.
530,596 km2 for 247-231, bbox north to 36.2 N: Lu 'conquered by King Kaolie in 249 BC'; Cliopatria's Lu row ends 248.
530,242 km2 for 230-226: 350 km2 less; Qin's conquest of Han in 230 ('King An of Han surrendered and Han came under Qin control') redraws the northern neighbour; no Chu event.

correction.text: the shape as drawn, valid to 223 BC ('Conquered by Qin: 223 BC'), not 224; years only

keyframe_review.note: 529,864 km2 for 225-224: Wei's fall in 225 ('King Jia of Wei surrendered') redraws the neighbour. Cliopatria ends Chu in 224; the pages end it in 223 ('In 223 BC, Wang Jian conquered the Chu capital Shouchun and captured King Fuchu of Chu'), so the shape holds one year longer. In 224 Li Xin 'captured Pingyu' and Meng Tian 'captured Qinqiu' before Xiang Yan destroyed their army: contested, not lost.

region.text: the viscounty at Danyang, 'located in today's Zhijiang, Hubei province' (or 'near present-day Xichuan County, Henan'), in the original Chu area (modern Hubei)

ledger.note: c. 1030: Xiong Yi founds Chu at Danyang. Infobox 'Founded by Xiong Yi: c. 1030 BC', 'Viscounty (before 704 BC)'; capital 'Danyang (c. 1030 – c. 680 BC)'. The core is Cliopatria's 750 shape cut to Hubei and Hunan, less the circles of E, Quan, Luo, Deng and Yong, which the ledger annexes later; the page names the capital, not a boundary.

863: Xiong Qu overthrows E. 'The Chu viscount Xiong Qu overthrew E in 863 BC.' The Chu page does not locate E. The Ezhou page (opened 2026-10-18) says the city's name 'derives from the nearby ancient Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BCE) vassal State of E' and gives the city at 30.39 N 114.89 E; E is drawn as a 50 km circle there, on the Yangtze below the Han mouth (the Nanyang basin, the other site in the usual accounts, is on no page). The year is the Chu page's and the place the researcher's reading of 'nearby', confidence 2; the first version drew 70 km at Wuhan at confidence 1.
704: Chu becomes a kingdom. 'Xiong Tong proclaimed king: 706 or 703 BC'; infobox 'Kingdom (704–223 BC)'. Same state, same colour; the nominal Zhou vassalage ends here (the Zhou dossier).
704: Quan annexed. 'Quan' heads the page's list of states annexed by Chu, dated 704 BC; Quan lay near modern Jingmen (the researcher's placing).

690: Luo annexed ('Luo', 690 BC, in the page's list; the Luo page: 'Conquered by Chu: 690 BC'). The Luo page names the capital 'Yicheng (宜城)', on the Han below Xiangyang, and also says 'Luo (today's Luoshan County, Henan Province)'; drawn as 35 km at Yicheng (112.26 E 31.72 N), the researcher's choice between the two. The first version drew 50 km at Xiangyang, which already contained Deng's circle.

689: the capital moves to Ying. 'sometime between 695 and 689 BC, the Chu capital moved south-east from Danyang to Ying'; King Wen ('689–677 BC') 'moved the capital to Ying' (infobox c. 680). Dated 689 to match the capital strip (reviewer ea-01-a).
688-680: Shen annexed ('Shen', 688–680 BC). Shen is the Nanyang basin (researcher's placing).
684-680: Xi annexed ('Xi', 684–680 BC). Xi lay at modern Xi County east of Xinyang (researcher's placing).

678: Deng annexed ('Deng', 678 BC; the Deng page: 'In 678 BCE King Wén of Chu conquered State of Deng'). The Deng page gives the site as 'Dengzhou (鄧州/邓州), Henan Province or Xiangfan (襄樊), Hubei Province' and says 'With the annexation of the States of Shen and Deng, the State of Chu extended its territory into the Nanyang Basin'; drawn by Xiangyang (Xiangfan), the researcher's choice between the two sites.
648: Huang annexed. 'In the summer of 648 BC, the State of Huang was annexed by the state of Chu.' Huang lay at modern Huangchuan east of Xinyang (researcher's placing).

region.text: the State of Cao, 'roughly the area of modern-day Dingtao County, Shandong Province'

ledger.note: c. 633: Cao in Chu's camp. 'About 630 it was a vassal or ally of Chu'; 'When Chu attacked Song, Jin made a diversionary attack on Cao' before Chengpu (632). The page says vassal or ally; the start year is set a year before Chengpu, confidence 1. The Battle of Chengpu page (opened 2026-10-18) has Jin 'marched south in the spring of the following year and occupied the States of Wey and Cao', 'both satellites of Chu', and gives no year for Cao's allegiance.

632: Jin crushes Cao after Chengpu. 'After Jin defeated Chu at the Battle of Chengpu in 632 BC, Jin crushed the State of Cao'; Chu's hold on Cao ends. The Chu page: 'the Chu kingdom lost their first major battle at the Chengpu in 632 BC'.
623: Jiang (江) annexed ('Jiang', 623 BC). Jiang lay near modern Zhengyang, between Zhumadian and Xinyang (researcher's placing); Zhumadian is not in the gazetteer yet.

622: Liao annexed ('Liao', 622 BC). Liao lay near modern Gushi on the upper Huai (researcher's placing). (Reviewer ea-01-a: region given as the coordinates of Fuyang, Anhui, because the gazetteer place Fuyang resolves to Fuyang, Zhejiang.)

622: Lù (六) annexed. The Chu page's table of annexed states: '622 BC Lù (六).', beside Liao the same year. Lù lay at modern Lu'an, Anhui (gazetteer place Luan = Liuan, 116.48 E 31.75 N, 40 km). The Lu'an page (opened 2026-10-18) says 'During the Xia and Shang Dynasties, Liu was a country south of the Huaihe River' and that the vassal states there 'became subordinate to Wu and Chu successively' but does not mention the annexation, so the year is the Chu page's and the place the researcher's reading, confidence 2. Not Lu (魯), which has its own dossier (lu).

617: Jiang (蔣) annexed ('Jiang (蔣)', 617 BC), near modern Huaibin on the Huai (researcher's placing). (Reviewer ea-01-a: region given as the coordinates of Fuyang, Anhui, because the gazetteer place Fuyang resolves to Fuyang, Zhejiang.)
611: Yong annexed ('Yong', 611 BC). Yong lay in the mountains of north-western Hubei around Zhushan (researcher's placing).
601: Shuliao annexed ('Shuliao', 601 BC), one of the Shu states between the Huai and the Yangtze in central Anhui (researcher's placing).
574: Shuyong annexed ('Shuyong', 574 BC), another Shu state in central Anhui (researcher's placing; same area as Shuliao).
538: Lai annexed ('Lai (賴國)', 538 BC). Location not given; placed on the upper Huai near Xi County, confidence 1.

region.text: the State of Chen, made 'a prefecture of Chu'

ledger.note: 534: King Ling annexes Chen. 'In 534 BC, the State of Chen suffered internal disorder'; 'King Ling made Chen a prefecture of Chu, destroyed its ancestral temple and took Wu back to Chu' (the conversion itself undated on the page). Chen's dossier records the loss.

531: King Ling annexes Cai. 'In 531 BC, King Ling tricked and captured Marquis Ling of Cai, blamed him for killing his own father'; his brother Qiji 'was made Duke of Cai'. Cai's dossier records the loss and its move to Xincai.

529: Chen restored after King Ling's fall. 'In winter 529 BC, King Ling set off to attack the State of Xu'; 'the king had committed suicide'. The pages opened do not date the restoration under King Ping; Chen's ruler table resumes with Duke Hui 529–506 BC (Chen page). Confidence 1. The King Ping of Chu page (opened 2026-10-18) is silent on the restoration.

529: Cai restored at Xincai. Not on the pages opened (the King Ping of Chu page, opened 2026-10-18, is silent): the Cai page dates the move 'to Xincai (lit. "New Cai") in 531 BC' and its ruler table resumes with Marquis Ping 530–522 BC. Chu keeps Shangcai, which it gained in 531 and which stays in the Chu shape afterwards; only the restored Cai's seat at Xincai is given up. On the map this loss changes nothing, because Chu's own ledger never gained Xincai before 529; Chu takes Xincai in 493, when Cai leaves it for Xiacai. Confidence 1.
512: Xu annexed ('Xu', 512 BC). Cliopatria keeps an Xu row to 285, which this contradicts; the region is Xu's Cliopatria shape.

region.text: Chu's capital at Ying and the Jianghan plain around it

ledger.note: 506: Wu takes Ying. After the battle of Boju 'the Wu army captured Ying'; 'King Zhao of Chu escaped first to Yun, and then to the state of Sui'; infobox 'they captured and destroyed the Chu capital, Ying'. The Chinese-calendar date ('the 19th day of the 11th month') is not converted to a month. Hatched (rule 4); Wu's dossier should record the reverse.
505: Chu recovers Ying. 'In 505 BC, the Qin and Chu armies jointly defeated Wu in several battles'; 'King Zhao of Chu then returned to the capital Ying.'
504: the court moves briefly to Ruo. 'he temporarily moved the capital into the territory of the former state of Ruo' (504 BC); the infobox keeps Ying to 278, so the capital dot stays at Ying.

493: Cai leaves Xincai for Xiacai and the land at Xincai is taken as Chu's. 'later to Xiacai (lit. "Lower Cai") at present-day Fengtai County in Anhui' (Cai page, no year; the King Zhao of Chu page, opened 2026-10-18, is silent on Cai). Mirror of the Cai dossier's 493 loss; year and taker are both bridged, confidence 1. It is also why the Chu shape of 480 holds Xincai.

region.text: the part of Cliopatria's Chu shape of 480 that the ledger's gains do not cover: southern Henan, Anhui and the edges of Shaanxi, Chongqing and Jiangsu

ledger.counterpart: Dao, Ruo, Zhongli, Sui and other unnamed states of the Huai valley
ledger.note: c. 480: a bridge, not a dated event. The Chu page says only that Chu, after absorbing states in modern Hubei, 'then it expanded into the north towards the North China Plain', and its table lists Dao ('after 643 BC'), Ruo ('after 622 BC'), Zhongli ('Sometime in the 6th century BC') and Sui ('after 506 BC') without a firm year. Cliopatria's 480 shape (identical to its 750 and 700 shapes) holds this land, about 165,000 km2 in the gazetteer's cells (Henan 92,000, Anhui 55,000, Shaanxi 9,000, Chongqing 7,000, Jiangsu 4,000). The 750 and 700 keyframes now leave it out because no page dates it, so the 480 keyframe brings it in; the year is the handoff to Cliopatria's shape, a placeholder, confidence 1. The ledger's gains from 688 to 512 (Shen, Xi, Huang, Jiang, Liao, Lu, Jiang, Shuliao, Shuyong, Lai, Xu) are already subtracted.

region.text: Chen, 'fourteen cities in modern-day Henan and Anhui' at its peak

ledger.note: 479: Chen annexed. 'Chu annexed Chen in 479 BC'; the Chen page: 'It was finally unified with the Chu in 479 BC' (its ruler table ends 478). Chen's dossier ends here.

region.text: Cai at Xiacai, 'present-day Fengtai County in Anhui'

ledger.note: 447: Cai conquered. Chu 'overran Cai to the north in 447 BC'; the Cai page: 'In 447 BC, King Hui of Chu conquered Cai completely, but allowed the marquesses to settle near Changde'. Cai's dossier ends here.
445: Qi (杞, Henan) annexed ('Qi (Henan)', 445 BC); placed at Qi County east of Kaifeng (researcher's placing).
431: Ju annexed ('Ju', 431 BC), south-eastern Shandong around modern Juxian (researcher's placing); this is the shape's northern reach to 35.8 N.
After 418: Pi annexed ('Pi', 'After 418 BC'); northern Jiangsu near modern Pizhou (researcher's placing); the year is the page's lower bound, confidence 1.
c. 348: Zou annexed ('Zou', 'About 348 BC'). Zou is Cliopatria's 'Zhu' (邾/鄒) row, which ends 405; its shape is the region.

region.text: Yue's land taken by Chu in the partition with Qi

ledger.note: 333: Yue partitioned. 'Yue was partitioned by Chu and Qi in 333 BC' (infobox 'Conquered by Chu: 333 BC'; the Chu page: 'in either 334' or 333). The pages do not say which land went to Chu; the region is the part of Yue's last shape inside Cliopatria's 333 Chu shape (the former Wu lands to the coast). 'After the fall of Yue, the ruling family moved south to what is now northern Fujian and set up the Minyue kingdom' (Cliopatria's Minyue row from 333).

312: Hanzhong lost to Qin (bridge). Fx-52 (K05) re-check, 3 Nov 2026: the sentences earlier quoted here ('In 313 BC, Qin's strategist Zhang Yi tried driving a wedge between Chu and Qi', 'became known together as the battles of Danyang and Lantian', 'Qin then seized Hanzhong', 'Qu Kai was captured, while his 80,000 troops were beheaded') are not on the King Huai of Chu page as served (about 480 words: reign 328-299 BC, 299 hostage, 296 death), and no page opened (King Huai of Chu, Hanzhong, Zhang Yi, King Huiwen of Qin, the Timeline of the Warring States, earlier Chu (state), Warring States period, Qin (state)) names the battles or the seizure. Dated on the pages: the Timeline has '312 BC: Qin defeats a Chu army' (no place); the Zhang Yi page has, after the 'six hundred li' deception, 'Chu went to war with Qin. Qin defeated Chu and demanded a further six hundred li of land' (no year). So Qin's defeat of Chu in 312 is dated, but that Chu held Hanzhong and lost it then is the researcher's reading, confidence 1 (the floor), a bridge matching qin/ledger/19. Cliopatria's Chu shapes -404 to -284 hold none of Hanzhong's 87 cells (80 km disc), so the compiler moves no Chu cell; the Qin -315 keyframe leaves Hanzhong out until the 312 gain.

301: Chongqiu (Zhongqiu) lost. King Zhaoxiang of Qin page: 'In 301 BC' Qin, Han, Wei and Qi allied to attack Chu; the Chu army was defeated 'at Zhongqiu (重丘)' and the Chu general Tang Mei was killed. The page records a victory, not a seizure of land, and gives no location; 'seized Chongqiu of Pingyuan Commandery' is not on it (nor on the King Huai of Chu page as served, about 480 words: fx-52 K05). The gain, and the 50 km disc round Nanyang, are the researcher's reading: confidence 1. fx-54 (3 Nov 2026): re-sourced from King Huai of Chu to King Zhaoxiang of Qin.

region.text: eight Chu cities on the Qin frontier

ledger.note: 299: eight cities lost (the researcher's count). No page opened dates 'eight Chu cities': the King Huai of Chu page as served does not have the sentence (fx-52 K05), and the Chu (state), Warring States period, Timeline of the Warring States and King Zhaoxiang of Qin pages do not have it. King Zhaoxiang of Qin page: 'In 300 BC' Mi Rong was sent to 'capture Xiangcheng (襄城)', killing 30,000 soldiers and the Chu general Jing Que; 'in 299 BC King Huai of Chu was forced to go to Wu Pass (武關) to negotiate terms with Qin' and was abducted and taken to Xianyang; he refused to cede the Wu and Qianzhong commanderies and 'was detained as a hostage'; Qin 'proceeded to invade Chu the next year, capturing 16 cities and killing 50,000 Chu soldiers' (the year is only implied, 298). The count of eight, the year 299 and the frontier band are the researcher's reading; no page opened dates them: confidence 1. fx-54 (3 Nov 2026): re-sourced to King Zhaoxiang of Qin, confidence 2 to 1.

region.text: Song's land taken by Chu in the partition with Qi and Wei

ledger.note: 286: Chu's share of Song. 'In 286 BC, King Min of Qi plotted with the states of Chu and Wei for a joint expedition against Song'; 'Finally, Song was partitioned by Qi, Chu and Wei' (the Song page: 'annexed by Qi in 286, with troops from Chu and Wei serving on behalf of Qi'). The pages do not name Chu's part; the region is the part of Song's last shape inside Cliopatria's 284 Chu shape. Cliopatria dates it 284.

region.text: Ying and the western lands of Chu taken by Bai Qi

ledger.note: 278: Bai Qi takes Ying. 'In 278 BC, he led the Qin army to capture Ying (郢), the capital city of Chu', 'Reportedly drowning 100,000 people in a flood attack'; rewarded with the title Lord Wu'an. The Qin's wars page: 'In 278 BC, Qin forces led by Bai Qi attacked Chu from the former Ba and Shu territories, capturing the Chu capitals of Ying and Chen' (Chen was the refuge, not a capture; the Chu page's infobox makes Chen the capital 278–241). The region is what Cliopatria removes between its 284 and 277 shapes: the Jianghan plain west of 110.4 E, Qin's Nan Commandery in the usual accounts. The King Qingxiang of Chu page (opened 2026-10-18) is silent on Yan, Deng, Yiling, the Nan Commandery and Qianzhong; it dates only King Huai's hostage episode of 299.
278: the court flees to Chen (Huaiyang). Infobox 'Chen (陳) (278–241 BC)'; 'After the destruction of the old Chu capital at Ying, Chen became the Chu capital' (Chen page).
249: Lu conquered. Lu 'conquered by King Kaolie in 249 BC'. Cliopatria's Lu row ends 248; its last shape is the region.
241: the capital moves to Shouchun. 'Chu moved its capital east to Shouchun, farther away from the threat of Qin'; infobox 'Shouchun (241–224 BC)'.

region.text: Pingyu and Qinqiu and the Chu–Qin frontier

ledger.note: 224: Qin invades. Ying Zheng ordered Li Xin and Meng Tian 'to lead 200,000 troops to attack Chu'; 'Li Xin captured Pingyu while Meng Tian captured Qinqiu', then 'Most of the Qin forces under Li Xin were destroyed in the battle' by Xiang Yan; Wang Jian then took 600,000 men and 'Xiang Yan was killed in action' (the page places these two years after 226). Blend over the Chu–Qin frontier until Shouchun falls.
223: the war ends with Chu's conquest. 'In 223 BC, Wang Jian conquered the Chu capital Shouchun and captured King Fuchu of Chu'.

region.text: the whole kingdom, Shouchun and all

ledger.note: 223: Qin conquers Chu. 'In 223 BC, Wang Jian conquered the Chu capital Shouchun and captured King Fuchu of Chu, shortly after Lord Changping was defeated and killed by Qin forces under Meng Wu'; 'By then, Chu had been completely conquered by Qin.' The Chu page: 'Conquered by Qin: 223 BC'. The Wu-Yue lands were attacked 'The following year'. Cliopatria ends Chu in 224.

wars.name: Zhou–Chu War
wars.outcome: King Zhao of Zhou's second southern campaign 'ended with King Zhao losing his armies and his own life' in the Han River region; no border moved.
wars.note: The Western Zhou page dates it: 'until the disastrous Zhou–Chu War in 977 BC'; the Chu page mentions King Zhao's 'campaign against Chu' without a year.

wars.name: Battle of Chengpu
wars.outcome: 'the Chu kingdom lost their first major battle at the Chengpu in 632 BC'; Jin's hegemony. Cao ('a vassal or ally of Chu') was crushed by Jin afterwards; Chen fought 'as an ally of Chu at the Battle of Chengpu' (Chen page). No Chu land changed hands.

wars.name: Battle of Bi
wars.outcome: 'In 597 BC, Jin was defeated by Chu in the battle of Bi'; King Zhuang's hegemony; no border moved.

wars.name: Wu–Chu war and the Battle of Boju

zones.text: Ying and the Jianghan plain, occupied by Wu 506-505

wars.outcome: 'The Wu were victorious, and they captured and destroyed the Chu capital, Ying' (506); 'In 505 BC, the Qin and Chu armies jointly defeated Wu in several battles' and 'King Zhao of Chu then returned to the capital Ying.'
wars.note: 'Wu was joined by the minor states of Cai and Tang'. Hatched occupation, not a change of owner (ledger).

wars.name: Chu's partition of Yue
wars.outcome: 'Yue was partitioned by Chu and Qi in 333 BC' and 'conquered by Chu in 333 BC' (Yue page); the Yue house withdrew to Fujian as Minyue. A later Chu campaign against Yue in 306 BC (earlier credited to the King Huai of Chu page, which as served does not have it: fx-52 K05) is on no page opened: the Chu (state), Warring States period and Yue (state) pages do not date it (the Chu page has Chu defeating Yue in 'the late 4th century BC' without a year), so nothing is drawn for 306 (fx-54, 3 Nov 2026).

wars.name: Qin-Chu war of 312 BC
wars.outcome: Chu lost a field army to Qin in 312 BC (Timeline page: 'Qin defeats a Chu army', no place named); the loss of Hanzhong is the researcher's reading, not a dated sentence on any page opened.
wars.note: Renamed in fx-52 (K05): 'Battles of Danyang and Lantian', 'Qin then seized Hanzhong' and the 313 deception are not on the King Huai of Chu page as served, and no page opened names them; the span is now the single dated year 312 (it was 313-312).

wars.name: Battle of Chuisha (Chongqiu)
wars.outcome: 'In 301 BC' Qin, Han, Wei and Qi allied against Chu and beat the Chu army 'at Zhongqiu (重丘)', killing the general Tang Mei (King Zhaoxiang of Qin page). The page does not name the battle or the place, and has no seizure of land: the zone is the researcher's reading (fx-54, 3 Nov 2026).

wars.name: Bai Qi's campaign against Chu

zones.text: Ying and the Jianghan plain west of 110.4 E

wars.outcome: 'In 278 BC, he led the Qin army to capture Ying (郢), the capital city of Chu'; the court fled to Chen. The Battle of Yanying page would not load; the 279 campaign (Yan, Deng, Yiling) is not on the pages opened.

wars.name: Qin's conquest of Chu (Qin's wars of unification)
wars.outcome: Li Xin's 200,000 destroyed by Xiang Yan after taking Pingyu and Qinqiu (224); Wang Jian's 600,000 kill Xiang Yan; 'In 223 BC, Wang Jian conquered the Chu capital Shouchun and captured King Fuchu of Chu'; the Wuyue region attacked in 222.
wars.note: Infobox of the whole war: 230–221 BC.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line: Spring and Autumn and Warring States frontiers are approximate throughout; the Han, Huai and Yangtze valleys are the only natural anchors.

notes:
Cliopatria rows to correct (keyframe_review): the 750 and 700 shapes (353,000 km2 to 34.7 N, identical to the 480 shape) are Chu at the end of the Spring and Autumn period, which pushes Cai and Chen 80-120 km north of Shangcai and Huaiyang in Cliopatria; the keyframes now carry only the Hubei and Hunan core to 481 and the ledger rebuilds the rest (see the repair pass); Chu ends 223, not 224; Chen (479) and Cai (447) are added only in 450; Song's share only in 284. Cliopatria's Xu row runs to 285 though the Chu page annexes Xu in 512; Cliopatria's Wu row runs to 451 though Yue 'destroyed and annexed Wu in 473 BC' (Yue page); Cliopatria's Zhu row (ends 405) is the Zou the Chu page annexes c. 348.

Pages that would not load: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Yanying (URL not found); Bai Qi's page replaced it and gives only the 278 capture of Ying, so Yan (279), Deng, Yiling, Nan Commandery and Qianzhong (277) are not in the ledger. The Qin's wars page says Bai Qi captured 'Ying and Chen' in 278; the Chu page makes Chen the capital 278-241, so 'Chen' there is the court's refuge.

Gaps the reviewer should expect: the states annexed in the 8th-6th centuries (Quan, Luo, Shen, Xi, Deng, Huang, Jiang, Liao, Yong, Shuliao, Shuyong, Lai) are dated by the Chu page but located by the researcher (confidence 2, radius regions; Zhumadian is not in the gazetteer); E's site is disputed (confidence 1); the losses to Qin of 312, 301 and 299 are at confidence 1 (the King Huai page dates only the surrounding events); the 306 campaign against Yue has no land named; the 598 and 534-529 Chen episodes and King Ping's 529 restorations are not on the pages opened; Battle of Yanling has no year on the Chu page and is left out of wars; vassal relations with Chen and Cai before their annexation are called 'ally' by the pages and are not drawn.

Counterparts: wu should record the 506-505 occupation of Ying; xu, zhu, lu, yue, song, chen, cai should carry the matching losses; the E, Quan, Luo, Shen, Xi, Deng, Huang, Jiang, Liao, Yong, Shu, Lai, Qi (杞), Ju, Pi, Tang states have no Cliopatria rows (listed in the report). Danyang: the page gives Zhijiang (Hubei) and Xichuan (Henan); the capital dot is at Zhijiang.

Repair pass (2026-10-18, after the reviewer's fail): (1) chu_-1030, chu_-750 and chu_-700 no longer contain the Hubei states the ledger annexes later (E 863 is cut from the 1030 shape only; Quan 704, Luo 690, Deng 678 and Yong 611 are cut until their years), and chu_-700 is the Hubei and Hunan core, not the whole end-of-period shape. (2) The part of Cliopatria's shape that no page dates (about 165,000 km2, mostly Henan and Anhui; Dao, Ruo, Zhongli and Sui are annexed in the Chu page's table 'after 643', 'after 622', 'in the 6th century' and 'after 506' BC) enters at 480 through a confidence-1 bridge entry, so the map shows Chu at about 260,000 km2 in 481 and 410,000 km2 in 480 (gazetteer cells, which run about 19% above Cliopatria's own areas); the jump is Cliopatria's, not an event. (3) Added Lù (六) 622 (Lu'an), the 493 gain of Xincai, and Zhoukou in the chu_-480 cut. (4) Re-placed E (Ezhou page) and Luo (Luo page, capital Yicheng). Jiang (蔣) 617, Shuyong 574 and Lai 538 add no new land on the map because their circles lie inside those of Liao, Shuliao and Huang; their pages give no separate extent. (5) Pages opened and silent: King Ping of Chu (529), King Zhuang of Chu (598 Chen, Dao/Ruo/Zhongli/Sui), King Qingxiang of Chu (279-277), King Zhao of Chu (Cai 493); Marquis Ping of Cai does not exist as a page (URL not found). The Chu page does not mention Cao, King Zhuang's 598 annexation of Chen, or the 306 campaign against Yue beyond the King Huai page's line. Reviewer's 'Fuyang' coordinates and the 689 Ying move were applied by the reviewer and kept. fx-54 (3 Nov 2026): the 301 (Chongqiu/Zhongqiu) and 299 (eight cities) Qin-Chu events are re-sourced to the King Zhaoxiang of Qin page, which dates the 301 victory at Zhongqiu, the 300 Xiangcheng and the 299 Wu Pass hostage; no page opened has 'eight cities' (confidence 1), a 306 Chu attack on Yue or Shaoling in 311.
